quote: To form accurate beliefs about something, you really do have to observe it
content: The physical core of this claim has held up well. The thermodynamic cost of information processing, that erasing one bit dissipates at least kT ln 2 of heat (Landauer's principle), was directly measured by Bérut et al. (2012), and the converse, extracting work from information via a Szilárd-type engine, was demonstrated by Toyabe et al. (2010). So "engines of cognition" paying a real thermodynamic price is not metaphor; it is confirmed physics. The caveat is that the sweeping epistemological moral, that you cannot form accurate beliefs without doing work, rests on using Landauer's principle to exorcise Maxwell's demon, and that exorcism remains philosophically disputed: John Norton argues the principle is neither cleanly derivable from statistical mechanics nor sufficient on its own to rescue the Second Law without circularity (Earman & Norton 1999).

Calling the Second Law "essentially Bayesian" adopts the Jaynes/MaxEnt program, the interpretation of thermodynamic entropy as missing information relative to an observer, as if it were settled fact. It is an influential but minority interpretive stance, not a consensus. Many physicists hold that Boltzmann/Gibbs entropy is an objective property of a system's macrostate and that the identification with a knower's subjective uncertainty is a philosophical add-on, criticized precisely for letting the Second Law's status depend on what someone happens to know (the same "isn't that too subjective?" objection raised in Beautiful Probability, here turned around). The underlying theorem (Liouville's, phase-space volume conservation) is real; the gloss that this makes entropy fundamentally epistemic is a contested reading presented as the plain meaning.
